transcript: Chapter Two, What the Road Brought They went into the cut at first light with the order of March worked out the night before, twice, out loud, until even Milo could say it back. Garrick at the head, on foot, with Tuck's rope in his left hand and nothing in his right. Dessa forty paces ahead of him, because Dessa saw things at a distance and it was a waste to put her anywhere else. Marta at the near wheel, Milo at the off wheel with the drag chain in his fist. Torrin behind the tailgate, and Wyke up on the tailgate itself, facing backward, with a length of iron bar across his knees. Senna rode. Senna had argued about riding for eleven minutes and had lost, which she noted was the first argument she had lost since 2141. Forty minutes, Garrick said. We do not stop. If something needs picking up, it stays where it fell. If the mule balks, we push. Wyke, looking backward. That's the whole job. You look backward and you say what you see out loud, even if it's nothing, especially if it's nothing. Garrick swept his eyes down the line one more time. Nobody lights anything unless I say. They come at it. You put out an edge in a closed place like that, and every one of them inside a mile will know exactly where you're standing. Milo raised a hand. What if? Then I'll say it, Garrick said, and you'll hear me. The south mouth of the cut swallowed them the way a door swallows a room. Torrin had expected it to be dark. It was not dark. It was worse than dark. It was a flat, even, shadowless gray. The walls went up eighty feet on both sides. The sky lay overhead in a long strip of milk, and nothing in the place threw a shadow in any direction. The rock was pale and layered and shot through with old drill marks, perfect vertical half cylinders in a row, cut by a machine no one alive could have built or repaired. Somebody had put a fortune into taking eighty feet of ridge out of the road's way. That somebody had been dead a hundred years. The road was still here, and so were the drill marks. The cartwheels changed their sound. Out on the open road, they had hummed. In here, each turn came back off both walls a half second late. Torrin pasted off in his head. It was the only thing he had. Twenty, fifty, a hundred. At a hundred and forty, the east wall broke. A gully came down it at an angle. A washed out scar of loose scree and broken shale where a farm track had crossed the ridge before anyone cut a road through it. Above the gully, the bank went back in steps. A person could get up it. A person could not get a cart up it. Not with an hour and a winch. He marked it anyway, the way his father had taught him without ever saying he was teaching him. One way out that isn't a mouth. A hundred and forty in from the south. At a hundred and eighty, the west wall had a square hole in it at road level. Four feet on a side. Concrete. Half filled with silt. A drain that took the ridge's water under the road and out the other side. Wet air came out of it. It smelled like cold stone and standing water. At two hundred and ten, near the north mouth, the west wall had dropped a slab. It had come down long ago. Grass grew on it. It had taken most of the north end of the roadway and left a gap on the east side about eight feet wide, with the wall on one hand and forty tons of broken limestone on the other. Garrick stopped the mule twenty paces short of it. Dessa, he said. She was already at the gap, standing sideways to it the way she stood at everything, looking through at the light on the far side. Clear, she said. Road runs out onto the flat. There's a dead poplar about a hundred yards on. Any dust? No dust. Milo, chain off. We're taking it through one wheel at a time. Wyke, stay up and keep. There's something in the road behind us, Wyke said. He said it in exactly the voice he used for everything. Torrin turned around with his heart still at its ordinary speed, because Wyke's voice had given him no reason to do otherwise. Ninety yards back, in the flat gray light, a man was walking up the middle of the cut. Except the walk was wrong. The legs went straight, and the feet came down on their outer edges, and the whole weight of the thing came forward each time in a way that a body with a plan in it does not move. Except it had no face. It had a head. The head. The head had no arrangement on the front of it, just gray, crowded, the color of wet ash, like a shape somebody had started and then set aside. Husk, Garak said. The word went through Torrin's stomach and out the other side. His father let go of the mule's rope and walked back down the line past Marta, past Milo, past Torrin. Not hurrying. And Torrin saw him roll his left sleeve as he came, one turn the way he did it every morning of his life. The husk came on at its steady, wrong, straight pace. One is a nuisance, Garak said, to nobody in particular in the voice he used on the gate. One is a nuisance. Watch this, and then stop being frightened of it. Twelve feet out he put his edge on. Torrin had seen it a thousand times and it still did something to the back of his neck. The dark pin at his father's wrist opened along its seam and ran, and there was a blade off the back of Garak's hand. Long, clean, single-edged, blunt-backed, as ordinary as a shovel and about as fussed over. The husk ran the last four feet. Garak stepped off the line of it, turned his hips, and put the blade through where a collarbone would be. The thing came apart. There was no blood, because there was nothing in it to bleed. It went to gray ash from the wound outward in about a half second. A dry collapse with a sound like a sack of flour dropped on a floor, and the ash hung in the still air of the cut, and then began, slowly, to settle. That's it, Garak said. That's the whole of it. They're not strong, and they're not clever, and one solid hit finishes them. And I have killed perhaps four hundred of these things on a gate and never once been hurt by one. Milo in a small voice. You said one is a nuisance. I did. What's more than one? More than one, said Garak, is why we're going to get this cart through that gap in the next four minutes. They did not get four minutes. The second husk came out of the drain. It came out headfirst and flat, dragging itself through the silt like something being born, and it was up and walking before the third one's arms were through the hole behind it. Torrin heard Dessa say a number, four in a voice gone absolutely level. Then she said six. Then she stopped saying numbers. They came out of the drain in a line. They came down the last forty yards of the north cut, through the gap, around the slab, in a slow crowd that filled the eight-foot space and kept filling it. Torrin looked south. The south was not empty either. Behind them, where there had been one husk and a spreading patch of ash, there were now nine. Beyond the nine, the cut ran back two hundred yards to the mouth, and the mouth was gray with movement. Marta. Garak said, I have it. Marta Faust stepped back from the wheel, put her feet a little apart, and set her hands out at waist height with the palms turned down, the way a woman settles a sheet onto a bed. Something happened in the air behind the cart. Torrin felt it before he saw it, and he never afterward found the right words for either. There was a pressure, a thickening. The light forty feet south of them went very slightly wrong, the way heat over a stone goes wrong, and the sound out of that direction dropped by half. The first husk to reach it walked straight into nothing at all and stopped, as though it had walked into the side of a house. Oh, Milo said. Mum. Eyes forward, love. But you never. Eyes forward. Torrin had known Marta Faust since before he could remember. She had set his wrist when he was six. She had made the poultice that got his grandmother through the winter of the bad cough. She had never in his whole life done a single thing that looked like this. And he understood, with a strange cold clarity, that she had been able to do it the entire time and it had simply never come up. Torrin, his father shouted. Edge! Here is what nobody tells you. It is not a thing you switch on. There is no switch. There is a warmth under your breastbone, small and low, about the size of a coin. You have had it for one day. Someone is shouting at you. Your hands are shaking. Your ears are full of a sound like a mill working. And somewhere inside all of that, you have to find the warmth and do something to it. Torrin reached for it. He reached the way you reach for a stuck jar lid, hard with everything. Gripping, he pulled at the warmth. He thought blade because a blade was what a person was supposed to have. His father had a blade. Every fighting man he had ever seen had a blade. He bore down on the picture of it with his whole mind. The ember got hot on his arm. The seam opened a fraction. Then the warmth under his breastbone guttered like a candle in a draft, and the seam closed. There was a plumstone of dark metal strapped to his forearm and nothing else. Torrin, I'm trying. He tried again. He got the same half inch of seam and the same guttering, and this time it hurt. A thin, unpleasant wrongness behind the ribs, like pulling a muscle in a place that has no muscles. A husk came around the near side of the cart. Milo was there. Milo had the drag chain. Milo, who had never hit anything in his life, and who apologized to the mule, swung it two-handed into the thing's knee. The chain went through. The leg came apart at the joint into a spray of ash. The husk pitched forward onto the road on one knee and one stump, and kept coming, on its hands, without any change in its speed or its attitude, because there was nothing in it that could be discouraged. It got a grip on Milo's boot. Torrin did not think about it. That was the whole of it, and he would not understand it for three months. He did not think. There was no blade in his mind and no shape in his mind, and nothing in his mind at all except his hands going forward toward Milo's foot. The ember opened. Metal ran up over the back of his hand and set. The weight of it came down at the end of his arm and dragged his wrist over. It was the hook. Fat, blunt-backed, poorly angled, deeply unimpressive. He swung it because it was there. The hook went past the husk's shoulder and caught it under the arm. Torrin's own momentum did the rest. The curve bit. The thing's grip tore off Milo's boot. The husk came off the ground and around and into the cart's wheel with a bang that shook the whole bed. It didn't come apart. It rolled. Torrin got the hook into it again in the back this time. And pulled it a yard down the road away from Milo. Wick came off the tailgate and put the iron bar through it, and it went to ash around the bar. Wick looked at the hook. Then it tore in. That's not a sword, he said. I know it's not a sword. I'm not complaining. Wick was already climbing back up. It's just not a sword. Garrick, Marta called. I can hold this end. Do something with the other one. I'm taking the gap. Torrin's father shouted back. Bring her up behind me. Torrin Wick. Wheels. Milo, get on the mule's head and don't let go of it. Then he walked north, alone, into the eight feet between the wall and the slab. Eight feet of road with forty tons of limestone on one side and a sheer rock wall on the other is a bad place to be. It is also, and this is the entire point, a place where only two things can reach you at once. Garrick made them come to him. He stood a yard back from the narrowest point with his weight low and his blade held short, and he let the gap do the arithmetic. Two came. He took the left one through the chest, stepped inside the right one's reach, and put his shoulder into it before the blade went in. Two more came over the ash of the first two. He took those. Two more. Torrin counted eleven before he made himself stop counting and start pushing. The cart came up the last twenty yards with the near wheel shrieking where the axle had gone dry. Milo hung off the cheek strap with both hands, talking to Tuck without pause, saying what a good old animal he was and how they were nearly out. Wick had the off wheel and Torrin had the near. The road under their boots had gone soft and slippery with a half inch of drifted ash. Four more yards, Garrick shouted. They got three of them. Then Dessa went up the slab. She did it without asking anybody, which was the whole of Dessa Cole in one movement, a three-foot scramble onto the tilted face of the fallen rock. One boot jammed in a seam, one hand flat on the stone, head and shoulders clear of the top and out into the open light of the north. She came down before Torrin had finished being frightened for her. Don't, she said. Dessa, don't take the cart through. She said it at Garrick, not at anyone else. There's about forty of them on the flat. They're coming around the outside of the slab, off the shoulder of the ridge, and they'll be at that gap from the far side in two minutes. She wiped her hand down her front. The road out there is open ground. No walls. Nothing to make them come at you two at a time. Torrin watched his father take that in. It took perhaps a second and a half. Garrick looked at the gap he had just paid eleven kills for, and out through it at the light, and back at the cart with his mother in it. Back her out, Garrick said. Back her. Back her out, Wick. They backed her out. It was the worst work of the day and none of it counted for anything. The cart had no reverse in it, so they lifted the tongue and walked it around and shoved her down twenty yards of ash they had just fought up. Every yard they gave back was a yard the husks took. Torrin put his shoulder into the tailgate with his boots skidding under him, and he did not look up, because there was nothing above him he wanted to see. When they stopped, they were back where they had started, in the middle of the cut, with a wall of husks north of them and a wall of husks south of them and Marta holding forty feet of the second one shut with her hands turned down. Right, Garrick said. He was breathing hard for the first time all morning. New plan. We hold here and we make them pay for it. Wyke, tailgate. Milo, off wheel. Torrin, near wheel. Dessa. Box seat, Dessa said already climbing. I'll call. You'll call. You'll call, Garrick agreed, and went north again. She called for four minutes and never once touched one of them. Six on the left, four more out of the drain. Left, left, Torrin, behind Milo. Good. Two on your grandmother's side, Wyke low. Marta, one's got through at the bottom. I see him, love. He's low, he's coming under. I see him. She stood on the box with nothing in her hands and no warmth at all under her breastbone, and she told five people where things were for four solid minutes. Once in the middle of it, he looked north and caught his father doing something he had never seen him do at the gate at Sallow Creek. Four of them came at Garrick together, spread across the width of the road, which meant the blade could only be in one place. So Garrick let the blade go out entirely, just dropped it. Gone. In the middle of a fight, which was the single most frightening thing Torrin had ever watched a person choose to do. A spear point came out in its place, longer by two feet, and went through the first one and into the second before the point had finished forming. Then the point went out too. Twin knives came up off both his fists, short and wide. The last two husks got inside his reach and discovered that inside his reach was the worst place in the cut to be. Three shapes, Torrin thought, with a kind of stupid pride in the middle of everything. Most people only ever get one. Torrin worked the near wheel and learned his trade in the worst classroom ever built. His father had been right about the shuffle. Torrin's first real mistake was a full step, taken fast, onto four inches of settled ash on hundred-year-old pavement, and his back foot went out from under him and dropped him onto his hip against the wheel hub. A husk had a fistful of his hair before he had finished arriving. It did not pull. It simply closed its hand and leaned, the way a door leans when the latch fails. Torrin's whole head went back. His neck lit up with a white line of pain. Milo came around the wheel and hid it in the elbow with the drag chain. The arm came apart. The hand stayed in Torrin's hair, gray and light and already crumbling. He tore it out along with a good deal of his own hair, threw it away from himself, and got his feet back. He did not take another full step for the rest of the day. Thank you, he said. You're welcome, said Milo. Do they ever stop? Do you want the true answer or the useful one? Useful. They stop in a minute. Good, Milo said, and swung the chain again. Torrin's hook went out and came back. Out and back. He caught one behind the knee and tipped it. Wick's bar finished it on the road. He caught a second under the arm and hauled it sideways into the wheel, and it broke on the iron rim. He reached for a third. There was nothing there to reach with. The warmth stuttered. The metal stayed shut. The husk got both hands on the cart's sideboard before Dessa shouted, and Wick came off the tailgate and took it in the back of the neck. Torrin, I'm trying. Then stop trying, Dessa shouted. That was the discovery, and he made it in the worst possible classroom. Every single time he tried, every time he set his jaw and reached and gripped and thought, now, come on, now nothing happened, or the seam opened a finger's width and closed again. And every time he stopped, every time something came at Milo or Dessa or the wheel and his hands went out ahead of his thinking, the metal ran and the hook was simply there, as though it had been waiting behind a door for him to stop leaning on it. So he built the only theory the evidence allowed. It isn't me. That was the shape of it, standing in the gray light with his arms starting to burn. It's the ember. It knows. It's older than my father and it has been in a drawer for 11 years and it knows what it's for. And when I grab at it, I'm getting in its way. The thought arrived with an enormous flooding relief. It meant the failures were not his fault. It meant there was something to do about them. What there was to do about them was get out of the way. He tested it. He stopped aiming. He let his arm go where the trouble was and did not look at the ember at all. The hook came. Every time. Torrin, his father shouted from somewhere up the north end, stop cutting with it. What? It's not a cutter. Pull. And that in the end was the second thing he learned in the cut. And this one was true. He stopped trying to chop. He put the hook out low, caught a husk behind the knee, and hauled using his hips the way you haul a full bucket up a well. The thing came off its feet and went down flat on the road. On the ground a husk was nothing at all. Weck's bar or Milo's chain or a boot heel finished it in a second. Torrin did it again. And again. He was not killing them. He was tipping them one after another and letting the others behind him do the finishing. The road at his feet went gray and deep with ash. For about 90 seconds, the three of them at the tail of that cart were actually, genuinely winning. That's a shape. Garruk roared from the dark. That's a shape, Torrin. Don't you dare go looking for a better one? It was the last thing his father ever said to him about the ember. Then the tactical problem changed, the way it always does. And it changed in the one direction they had not planned for. Marta's wall went up the road with her. She had been holding the south end, standing her ground 40 feet back from the tailgate. And Torrin had not once looked properly at what it cost her because there had been no spare second in which to look. When he finally did look, she was down on one knee with her palms still turned out. Her braid stuck to her neck. Her face had gone the gray of the walls. Marta. It's fine. Her voice came out with no air behind it. It's fine. It's only far. It's only that it's so far away from me. She got the knee up under her again. Tell Garruk I can hold 20 feet. Not 40. 20. 20 feet. Torrin shouted up the line. She can hold 20. His father's answer came back off both walls. Then we give her 20. Everybody south. To the gully. It was the right call and Torrin understood why in the same instant it was made. They could not go north. The gap at the slab measured eight feet and more husks came through it than the whole party could tip over in an hour. Nothing suggested the supply of them was running out. They could not stand where they were either because standing still against a swarm is simply losing slowly. What they had was 140 yards of road behind them and halfway along it, one gully in the east wall that a person could climb. The cart! Milo shouted. Turn it! They turned it. It took all six of them. Tuck did not want to and Tuck was the single bravest creature in that cut. The old mule had stood through the whole of it in a hail of settling ash with his ears flat back, and he had not once tried to bolt. He put his shoulders into the collar when Garruk pulled his head around. The cart came about in its own length with the near wheel screaming against the box. They started south at a run, with Marta moving backward at the tailgate, holding 20 feet of ruined air between them and the north. A hundred yards. His legs had stopped asking permission and his mouth had stopped doing anything useful. Sixty yards to the gully. Forty. That was when the warmth under his breastbone went out. Not guttered. Not flickered. It thinned, all at once. The way a stream goes to a trickle and then to wet stones. And the hook came apart in the middle of a pull and left him swinging his bare arm through a husk's shoulder. The thing hit him full in the chest and put him on his back on the road with a bang that emptied him. He lay there in four inches of ash, looking up at a strip of white sky 80 feet above him, and reached for the warmth, and there was nothing there to reach for. He was as empty as a turned out pocket. His arms would not close. His legs came back first. He got one knee under himself, and he was still on that knee when Week's hand closed on the back of his collar and hauled him up and forward without a word. The way you'd move a sack you needed somewhere else. Thirty yards, Dessa called. Marta, come on. I'm coming, love. Twenty, Tuck screamed. Torrin had never heard a mule make that sound. He would hear it for the rest of his life in the gray hour before waking at odd intervals for years. Something had come out of the drain mouth as they passed it. They had run right by the square hole in the west wall because there was no other road to run on. The old gray mule went down on his side in the traces. The cart's tongue snapped. The whole load slewed hard right across the road, and the off-wheel dropped into the drainage channel at the foot of the west wall and stuck. The cart stopped dead. The bed tipped. Senna made a sound inside the canvas once. They were thirty yards short of the gully. Torrin got his feet under him and turned around to look for his father and found instead that he was looking up. Because the gray had come over the top of the east bank. They were on the steps of the cut above the gully. A dozen of them, then twenty, coming down over the broken shale on the outsides of their feet with nothing in their heads at all. They came down the one climbable slope in two hundred yards of rock. The way out was above them. It was full. It was coming down.
